items.title: Are we witnessing an intelligence explosion?
items.summary:
From Luis Garicano and Alex Imas :

Hence AI capabilities improved 1.91 times faster after October 2025, but R&D spending grew 6.19 times and the technical workforce 3.10 times. So measured capability gains per dollar fell by approximately 69%, and measured gains per technical employee-year decreased by 38%. These figures are accounting; nothing causal can be inferred…

The accounting exercise we just did cannot tell us which. It shows that returns per dollar decreased: spending multiplied by 6.2 and the pace of progress by 1.9. But two different causes for this are possible. One is congestion: the effort is getting less productive as it increases, because it is hard organizationally to increase the budget by more than five times in a year. The other possibility is that each advance is harder than the last. With enough congestion, these same two numbers are even consistent with each advance making the next one easier, which is what an explosion requires. To know whether a break is needed, we must know what an unchanged relationship would have delivered…

In sum our finding is consistent with that of Bloom and his coauthors: ideas are getting harder to find in AI too, and maintaining the rate of improvement requires ever larger increases in inputs.

Overall the idea of an intelligence explosion still remains to be demonstrated.

The post Are we witnessing an intelligence explosion? appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION .
items.t: Are we witnessing an intelligence explosion?

items.title: The Economics of Rent Controls
items.summary:
I appear on Ryan Bourne’s excellent new podcast, The Economics of It . We discuss The Economics of Rent Controls drawing on my essay, Rent Control: The Ceiling Trap . It’s a very good discussion. Here’s one bit (edited slightly to remove some ums for reading and to fix a date I got wrong from memory):

RB: And in your essay you talk about some like truly insane ways that people are trying to signal to landlords that they’ll be good tenants in Oslo. I know you talk about that example.

Tabarrok: Yeah, so in Oslo they had rent controls for many years, but then they got rid of them in 1982 (fixed, AT), And there’s a great paper by Are Oust who looks at what happened. When the rent controls were in place, amazingly he found just like Friedman and Stigler found in San Francisco in 1906 that in Oslo the renters advertised I need an apartment, okay? Won’t you rent me an apartment? And as part of their advertisement they would say I’m willing to look after your cat, I’m willing to, you know, shovel the snow.

And on the other side the landlords would say, well, I’m looking for a good Christian. Uh you know, I’m looking for a uh a heterosexual, you know, single-family couple, whatever—these kinds of things. Sometimes literally advertised, sometimes this would happen, under the table. Um there would be things like you would have to pay uh months–sometimes years–you have to pay your rent years in advance. You know, all kinds of ways in which because of the shortage of apartments, it was the renters who had to advertise…

Even companies would say I’ve got a great employee. Please…
items.t: The Economics of Rent Controls

items.title: Do not overrate zero-sum status-seeking
items.summary:
If people really preferred relatively higher income in a poorer society, then those born in Western Europe and the US would be saving up their money so they could live like kings in Africa. Very few people of middle- or upper-class status in poor countries would try to get to the West. Obviously, what we observe is precisely the opposite. Doctors from Africa will come to America in order to drive a cab if their license to practice medicine isn’t recognized. Research on Middle Eastern and African migrants to Europe shows that they aren’t the poorest of the poor, but are relatively well off for where they come from. There are a lot of stories about how terribly South Asian migrant workers are treated in the Arab Gulf, but this causes no problem in recruiting laborers who want to earn a higher income.

Here is more from Richard Hanania .

items.title: The Everywhere Rent Seekers
items.summary:
Zidar and Zwick have a good post on the political power of billionaires versus the power of many millionaires, based on their excellent book The Everywhere Millionaire .

First, they point out that despite the attention given to (some days) trillionaires and billionaires, the combined wealth of the Everywhere Millionaires, the dentists, the car dealers, the mid-size business owners, is far larger.

…it’s important to put the scale of Forbes billionaire growth into perspective with the other rich and powerful actors in American society. Even at the very frothy public market valuations of the current moment, the Forbes list amounts to around $8 trillion or roughly 4.3% of total household wealth. Meanwhile, based on the most recent SCF, Everywhere Millionaires are probably worth more than $63 trillion or 38% of total household wealth.

Second, the power of the billionaires is often exaggerated relative to the power of the millionaires who have money and votes:

… Elon didn’t want the massive tax cuts in the OBBBA extended, which did not go to the tech billionaires. He didn’t benefit from the reduced EV demand, which came when the EV credits were abolished. He benefitted little from the new deduction for car loan interest passed in that bill, since financing car purchases is a small part of Tesla’s business.

Who drove these changes and reaped the rewards? The Everywhere Millionaire car dealers who reside in nearly every Congressional district and represent many of them directly. Elon lost big in the midterm election, despite spending half a billion dollars. Meanwhile, dozens…

items.title: Experimentally validated digital twins
items.summary:
There is a new paper by Raj Chetty, Jamie Fogel, Lawrence F. Katz, Kadeem Noray, Sonya Porter, and James Reisinger:

Modern program evaluation prioritizes evidence from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) because prior research found that observational estimates of program impacts often diverge substantially from experimental benchmarks. We revisit this finding — which was based on small survey datasets — in the era of large-scale administrative data. Using anonymized income tax records covering all American adults between 1999 and 2025, we estimate the effects of workforce training programs on earnings by using machine learning models to predict counterfactuals from rich data on prior work histories, demographics, and residential locations. Rather than testing whether our observational estimates are unbiased, we use 37 RCTs to estimate the distribution of their bias. We find that our machine learning estimates closely match the RCT estimates, with root mean squared error (RMSE) comparable to that of the RCTs themselves. Our method reduces RMSE by 60% relative to parametric estimators used in prior work because our larger samples and richer covariates permit more flexible, higher-dimensional models of the counterfactual. Applying our method to a broader set of sites and enrollment years beyond the experimental sample, we find that treatment effects on earnings vary substantially across locations and over time, even within a given program. Programs that place more participants into target-sector jobs generate the largest earnings gains, with impacts that persist even after…
items.t: Experimentally validated digital twins

items.title: Democrats’ US election sweep brings the price of their promised social contract into focus
items.summary:
‘The post-election wish list is about to run into harsh fiscal reality: there is no money’

Is this an opportunity for a new America? As the Reagan revolution four decades ago launched US society down the path to low taxes and meager solidarity, perhaps the Republican bloodbath last week could turn US politics toward building a new social contract anchored on an aspiration to equitable prosperity.

One can sense the ambition of the bumper new crop of Democrats ushered to power last week, calling for support for programs for children and their parents; emphatically endorsing the long-held dream of Medicare for All. The project includes rolling back Donald Trump’s cuts to Medicaid and food stamps, and restoring subsidies for health insurance under the Affordable Care Act that Republicans allowed to expire. And that’s just the start.
